slides.title: Kalaratri, the night that destroys fear
slides.sub: The seventh form of Durga, worshipped on Saptami

slides.title: The fiercest form
slides.body: Dark, wild-haired and fearsome, she destroys darkness, ignorance and fear itself. Despite her appearance she is called Shubhankari, the one who does good, because her ferocity protects.

slides.title: Three eyes, on a donkey
slides.body: She has a dark complexion, loose hair and three eyes, rides a donkey and holds a cleaver or sword and an iron hook. In Bengal today is Saptami, the morning of the Kola Bou's bath.

slides.title: Saptami: the day the clay comes alive
slides.sub: Prana pratishtha and the start of the main puja

slides.line: Dawn first: the Kola Bou is bathed and set beside Ganesha

slides.title: Prana pratishtha
slides.body: Prana pratishtha means establishing life. With mantras the priest invites the goddess to dwell in the clay image. Some traditions also ritually open the eyes. From here on the idol is the living deity.

slides.title: Every figure gets the puja
slides.body: Offerings go to Durga and to every deity of the image: Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesha, Kartik, the lion, and even Mahishasura. The day's bhog is cooked and offered.

caption.en:
Durga Puja 2026 Saptami in Kolkata: what prana pratishtha means 🪷

Saptami is Sunday 18 October, the first day of the main puja. After the Kola Bou's dawn bath, the priest invites the goddess into the clay image with mantras. From then on the idol is worshipped as the living deity.

The day's puja goes to every figure on the dais: Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesha, Kartik, the lion and even Mahishasura. In the evening comes sandhya arati, and in many pandals the first dhunuchi naach.

The order of these rites varies by family tradition and the panjika followed. Crowds are lighter in the morning than at night.

slides.title: Bhog: what goes on the plate and why
slides.sub: Offered to the goddess first, then shared with all

slides.title: Food for the goddess, then for all
slides.body: Bhog is food offered to the goddess. What remains becomes prasad, food carrying her grace, and it goes out to whoever has come. Usually vegetarian, and in many places cooked without onion or garlic.

slides.title: Five things on the plate
items: Khichuri: rice and lentils, ghee, whole spices
Labra: pumpkin, potato, radish and greens
Beguni: aubergine fried in gram-flour batter
Chutney: sweet and sour, often tomato

slides.title: Side by side, in rows
slides.body: The sharing is the point. In a sarbojanin puja, people of every background sit down side by side for the same khichuri, often from sal-leaf plates. Nobody asks who you are.

slides.title: No two pujas cook alike
slides.body: Some pujas serve plain rice, dal and chorchori instead of khichuri. Bonedi bari pujas keep their own menus, with luchi, fruit and home-made sweets. Treat the plate as typical, not fixed.

slides.title: Can visitors eat bhog?
slides.body: Many community pujas serve bhog to visitors on Ashtami or Navami: sometimes by coupon, sometimes free, sometimes only for the para. Ask at the puja office. Accept it with your right hand, and don't waste it.

slides.line: Khichuri, the heart of the plate

Durga Puja bhog in Kolkata: what goes on the plate and why it's shared 🍛

Khichuri, labra, beguni, a sweet and sour chutney and payesh. That's the classic plate. It's offered to the goddess first, and what remains becomes prasad, her blessing in edible form.

In a sarbojanin puja, people of every background sit down side by side for the same khichuri, and nobody asks who you are. The menu does vary from one committee or family to another, so treat this plate as typical rather than fixed.

slides.title: Bhoger khichuri, like Ashtami bhog
slides.sub: Gobindobhog, roasted moong, ghee. No onion or garlic

slides.title: Rice, dal and spices
items: ¾ cup (150 g) yellow moong dal

slides.title: Vegetables and the rest
items: 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp ground cumin
1 medium potato (150 g), peeled, 2 cm cubes

slides.title: Roast, wash, rest
slides.body: Dry-roast the moong dal over medium-low heat, stirring, for 6 to 8 minutes until light golden and nutty. Wash it with the rice in two or three changes of water, drain and rest 15 minutes.

slides.title: Fry the veg, temper the spices
slides.body: Fry potato and cauliflower in 2 tbsp ghee with a pinch of turmeric and salt for 4 to 5 minutes; lift out. Add 1 tbsp ghee, then the bay leaves, cumin, red chillies and whole spices for 30 seconds.

slides.title: Ginger, then rice and dal
slides.body: Add ginger and green chillies for 1 minute, then turmeric and ground cumin with 2 tbsp water for a minute. Stir in the rice and dal for 2 to 3 minutes. Add 5 cups hot water and the salt.

slides.title: Simmer and finish
slides.body: Boil, then simmer partly covered for 15 minutes. Add the vegetables, peas, sugar and last cup of hot water; cook 10 to 12 minutes. Off the heat, stir in the last 1 tbsp ghee and rest 5 minutes.

slides.title: Save this for Ashtami
slides.ask: Save it for your Ashtami bhog

caption.en:
Bhoger khichuri recipe: the Durga Puja Ashtami bhog, cooked at home for four 🍛

Gobindobhog rice and dry-roasted moong dal, simmered with ghee, ginger and whole spices. No onion, no garlic. You'll need about an hour.

Two things we'd tell any first-timer. Roast the dal only to light golden, because dark dal tastes bitter. And keep hot water by the stove: pandal-style khichuri should still flow off the spoon, and it firms up as it cools.

Save this for Ashtami morning 🙏
